methods.text:

text:
Brussels Sprouts.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn / Winter

Brussels sprouts form cabbage-like buds up a tall stem, ripening through autumn and winter. Freshly picked buttons have a sweet, nutty flavour; small, firm ones are good raw or cooked. Firm, fertile soil, careful transplanting and steady growth are the keys. Variety choice, poor soil or checked growth can produce open, leafy sprouts. Pick regularly and remove yellow leaves to keep the crop clean and usable from October into March.

Quick facts
Harvest

Nov – Feb

Germination

7–12 days

Sowing depth

3/4 in.

Row spacing

6 in. between seed rows

Yield per plant

2 lb

Plant spacing

24 in. each way

Sow

Mar–Apr outdoors. Start early varieties under cover in Feb–Mar.

Ready in

Early ~28 weeks; late ~36 weeks from sowing

Transplant

May–early Jul, when sturdy.

Recommended varieties
F1 HYBRID
Trafalgar F1

A later sprout with firm buttons for winter picking. A useful partner to an earlier-cropping variety.

F1 HYBRID
Brigitte F1

A modern Brussels sprout producing firm, well-shaped buttons. A strong candidate for the main autumn and winter crop.

F1 HYBRID
Maximus F1

An early-to-mid-season hybrid. Useful for starting the sprout harvest before later winter selections are ready.

F1 HYBRID
Crispus F1

A hybrid with clubroot resistance for affected plots. Continue using rotation and good growing conditions; resistance is not immunity.

Key risks
Club root (finger and toe)

Club root causes swollen, distorted roots, poor growth and wilting in warm weather.

Cabbage caterpillars

Cabbage white butterfly and moth caterpillars chew leaves and may shelter among developing sprouts.

Slugs

Slugs can damage young plants and older sprouts, especially in wet weather.

Frost

Extreme frost can damage older sprouts.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
30
BRASSICAS

Fertile soil and steady growth.

Add organic matter and let the ground settle before planting.

Choose sun and shelter.

Tall plants may need stakes where winds are strong.

Keep young plants weed-free.

Catch crops can use wide gaps only while sprouts are small.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, sheltered, fertile ground rich in organic matter. Work compost or well-rotted manure in deeply; firm the surface before planting.
Keep sprout plants clear of weeds; catch crops such as lettuce can use wide gaps while the plants are small.
Sowing & planting
Raise strong plants
Plant firmly
Sow 

Use a nursery bed for the main crop, or modules under cover for an early start. Cover the seed lightly and thin to one strong plant per cell.

Transplant 

Harden off plants raised under cover. Water the nursery row before lifting. Set sturdy plants 24 in. apart each way with their lowest leaves just above the soil. Firm well and water in.

Looking after the crop
Keep netting clear of the leaves to stop sparrows and pigeons reaching them.
Hoe young plants, then earth up stems for support. Firm soil; stake exposed plants.
Mulch dry or poor soil; checked growth raises the risk of open, blown buttons.
Remove yellow lower leaves before decay spoils sprouts beneath.
Check older plants for pests, leaf spots and frost damage.
Harvesting & storage
Pick tight buttons from the bottom upwards. Discard loose or damaged ones.
Pick regularly through the season and use the buttons promptly.
After button cropping, use tender shoots and leafy tops. Chop finished stems for compost by late spring.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Club root (finger and toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Use clean ground and tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Cabbage caterpillars	Chewed leaves; caterpillars.	Pick off eggs and caterpillars; cover with fine mesh.
Slugs	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk; remove yellow leaves around seedlings.
Frost	Cold-damaged older buttons.	Pick regularly; keep cut stems cool and frost-free.
Pigeons	Leaves pecked or stripped.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Cabbage root fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Fit collars or insect-proof mesh; rotate brassicas.
Final tips

Choose early and late varieties to extend winter picking.

Stake tall plants on windy sites.

Use tender leafy tops after button cropping.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 106–111 · Growing Techniques 150 · 167
